paras: The attempted lynching of Clifford Bell took place in Indianapolis, Indiana, on the evening of April 11, 1903, when a crowd of about a hundred men chased Bell, a young Black man, through the streets with cries of "lynch him." Policemen with drawn revolvers stopped the pursuit, and Bell escaped. A wire dispatch that called the episode a "race riot" carried the story to papers in Kentucky, Indiana and Wisconsin.
The dispatch described Bell as "a lad about twenty years old" and said the trouble began with a fight between him and two white men, without giving its cause.

According to the Indianapolis dispatch, the fight took place at about 5:30 in the evening. Bell was said to have struck one of the men, John Bush, on the head with a brick, knocking him senseless to the sidewalk. He then ran south, followed at first by about half a dozen men. As the chase went on the crowd grew to about a hundred, and cries of "lynch him" were heard as it pursued him through the streets. Policemen with drawn revolvers then intervened and saved him.
The coverage does not report an arrest of Bell or of any of his pursuers, a charge, or Bush's condition after the blow.

The story survives only in copies of one wire dispatch, first printed by the Louisville Courier-Journal on April 12 under "Mob After Negro Who Struck White Man at Indianapolis," with a subhead saying a "race war" would have followed but for the police. That version spelled the name "Clifford Ball," while the later copies read "Clifford Bell." On April 16 the River Falls Journal in Wisconsin cut it to one sentence in a "Later News" digest. The Jasper Weekly Courier, an Indiana weekly, ran the full text on April 17 under "Tried to Lynch Him."

Every version referred to Bell as "the negro" and gave the brick blow as fact, without naming a witness or police source. None of the copies found came from an Indianapolis paper, and no notice of the episode in the Black press appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Clifford Bell
bases: A crowd that grew to about a hundred men pursued Bell through the streets crying 'lynch him' until police with drawn revolvers saved him; no one was killed, so this is an attempted lynching (A2, A4).

Bell escaped and no death is reported (A2, A3, A4); the mob of about a hundred, acting without authority on the accusation that he had struck a white man with a brick, makes this an attempted lynching rather than a lynching under the standard definition (A2, A4).
All three articles are copies or digests of one Indianapolis wire dispatch with near-identical wording (A2, A3, A4); no local Indianapolis report or independent account was found.

accounts.label: Indianapolis wire report
accounts.gist: A fight between two white men and Bell ended with Bell striking John Bush with a brick and running; a crowd that grew to a hundred chased him crying 'lynch him' until policemen with drawn revolvers saved him.

framing.detail: The Courier-Journal headlined 'MOB AFTER NEGRO WHO STRUCK WHITE MAN AT INDIANAPOLIS' and credited the police with preventing a 'race war'; it states the brick blow as fact.
The Jasper Weekly Courier ran the full dispatch under 'Tried to Lynch Him' in its Indiana telegraph column.
The River Falls Journal reduced the story to one sentence in a 'Later News' digest, dropping the brick, Bush and the police.

conflicts.note: Same wire text; likely a typesetting or OCR variant. Two of three copies read Bell.

set_aside: Local court item, published the morning before the fight: a Clifford Bell, 'colored', locked up on a charge of receiving stolen goods in the Archibald clothing theft; not the mob episode, and nothing shows whether he is the same man.
